:::{#def-conjugate-transpose}
#### Conjugate transpose (Hermitian adjoint, Hermitian conjugate, transjugate)

The **conjugate transpose**
(also called the **Hermitian adjoint**, **Hermitian conjugate**, or **transjugate**)
of an $m \times n$ complex matrix $\matr{A}$
is the $n \times m$ matrix $\matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}}$
obtained by transposing $\matr{A}$ and then taking the complex conjugate of each entry:

$$(\matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk} \eqdef \overline{a_{kj}}
\quad \text{for } j \in \{1, \ldots, n\},\ k \in \{1, \ldots, m\}.$$

The conjugate transpose of a column vector $\vecf{z} \in \mathbb{C}^p$
is the $1 \times p$ row vector $\vecf{z}^{\mathsf{H}} = [\overline{z_1},\; \ldots,\; \overline{z_p}]$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-conjugate-transpose-notation}
#### Notation for the conjugate transpose

The operation is denoted variously across mathematics and physics:
$\matr{A}^*$ in pure mathematics (@axler2024linear [Definition 7.7, p. 231]),
$\matr{A}^{\dagger}$ ("$A$-dagger") in physics and quantum mechanics,
and $\matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}}$ in engineering, numerical linear algebra, and statistics.
These notes write $\matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}}$ because $^*$ is reserved for optimal points (as in $\vx^*$)
and $^{\dagger}$ frequently denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse in the broader literature.

The Hermitian adjoint matrix should not be confused with the classical *adjugate matrix*
(the transpose of the matrix of cofactors),
which older texts occasionally referred to as the "adjoint."

:::
